newsitem.title: USA: Budget deal possible Monday, Clinton says.
newsitem.headline: Budget deal possible Monday, Clinton says.

text.p: President Bill Clinton said on Sunday a wide-ranging budget and tax agreement with the Republican Congress could be completed as early as Monday if "remaining problems" were resolved.
Clinton described the emerging deal to balance the budget by 2000 and cut taxes by $85 billion as a "great opportunity."

His upbeat assessment of talks between the White House and Republican lawmakers came in a speech at a Democratic fund-raising dinner that raised more than $600,000 for the Democratic party's depleted coffers.

"I want us to make this balanced budget agreement tomorrow that I hope 90 percent plus of the Democrats will vote for," Clinton said at a $1,000-per-couple dinner for the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee.
"This is a very good budget if we can resolve the remaining problems," he said. "If we stay in a positive frame of mind. I think we have an excellent chance to get there."
Later, however, White House spokesman Joe Lockhart sought to soften the president's comments.
"They're back in tomorrow (talking), but I don't think that we have any clear indication that tomorrow is the day," Lockhart said after Clinton's speech.
"There's no timeline on it. They're going to go back in and talk tomorrow so there's always a possibility, but that was not a signal," he said.

But White House economic adviser Gene Sperling told Reuters the talks were now centred on "important issues such as who gets the tax cut and children's health care that are unresolved and critical to a sound balanced budget agreement."
"Nothing is agreed to on the tax package until everything is agreed to," he said.

In Washington, House Speaker Newt Gingrich sounded as optimistic as the president, telling reporters "virtually nothing" was left to resolve. Lawmakers said they expected to complete the talks by Monday night.

Clinton said the budget deal would provide for the largest increase for child health care since passage of the Medicaid programme for the poor in the mid-1960s and would restore almost all of the cuts in aid to legal immigrants imposed by last year's welfare reform bill.

The president has been keeping in close touch with the administration delegation negotiating the budget and tax deal with Republicans, which includes Sperling, Chief of Staff Erskine Bowles, Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin and Budget Director Franklin Raines.
In his remarks, Clinton indicated that one of the final sticking points involved differences between the White House and Republicans on how to structure the tax cuts.
"We are working hard to give people an appropriate tax cut without exploding the deficit," he said.
Congressional aides said both sides had made important concessions on contentious tax issues that had held up an agreement.

Republicans were expected to drop a provision that would not tax investment profits attributable to inflation. Clinton has strongly opposed that capital gains "indexing" plan, contending it could balloon the budget deficit in later years.
Clinton is due to address the annual summer meeting of the nation's 50 state governors on Monday in Las Vegas.
